platforms.title: That Morning Stiff Neck Might Be Low Magnesium
platforms.meta_description: Waking up with a stiff neck isn't just about posture — bending your head forward raises the load on your neck, and low magnesium keeps muscles from relaxing.
platforms.body_html:
Waking up with a neck that feels stiff and shoulders that feel like concrete is easy to blame on bad posture alone. But there's a second factor that matters just as much: how much magnesium is actually in your system.

The Steeper You Tilt Your Head, the More Your Neck Has to Hold

Research published by spine surgeon Dr. Kenneth Hansraj found that the average adult head weighs roughly 10 to 12 pounds, but tilting it forward to about 60 degrees pushes the load your cervical spine has to support up to around 60 pounds — more than five times the head's actual weight. That is not a small difference — it is the equivalent of carrying an extra bowling ball balanced at the top of your spine for hours at a time. Spend your day looking down at a phone or working with a low monitor, and your neck and shoulder muscles stay tense day after day, hour after hour, just holding up that inflated load without any real chance to fully rest.

Low magnesium makes the problem worse on top of that. Unlike calcium, which drives muscle contraction, magnesium is the mineral responsible for muscle relaxation, and when your body runs short, muscles tend to tip toward staying contracted and struggle to fully release. Tension around the neck and shoulders, along with eyelid twitching, is commonly cited as an early sign of low magnesium. So the load on your neck goes up, and the muscles carrying that load become worse at letting go — at the same time.

What Actually Helps With Neck and Shoulder Tension

First, hold your phone closer to eye level to cut down the angle your head has to tilt. Even shaving off 10 to 20 degrees meaningfully reduces the load your cervical spine carries. Second, work magnesium-rich foods — spinach, bananas, nuts — into your diet consistently rather than as an occasional afterthought. Third, roughly once an hour, take a few seconds to slowly turn your head side to side and shrug your shoulders up and down to keep the muscles from locking up between stretches.

Pillow height matters more than most people realize, too. A pillow that's too high keeps your neck bent forward all night long, which puts essentially the same load on it that looking down at a phone does while you're awake, just stretched across eight hours of sleep. Choosing a pillow height that lets your neck hold its natural, gentle curve while lying on your back can meaningfully ease that morning stiffness on its own.

If keeping up with all three feels like too much, start by thinking back to your stiffest recent morning and how long you'd been staring down at your phone the day before. If adjusting posture and adding more magnesium doesn't ease the tension, or numbness starts spreading down an arm, it's worth getting checked — that's no longer just ordinary muscle soreness, and a doctor can rule out a pinched nerve or disc issue that diet and posture changes alone won't fix.
